https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/08/15/toro.text: Menü Kereső Toroczkai szerint hangulatkeltés, a Fidesz szerint önfényező Facebook-bohóckodás volt Magyar Péter paksi tájékoztatója Belföld Madzin Emília Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Magyar Péter a szombati paksi élő bejelentkezéseiben többször megjegyezte, hiába hívta a parlamenti pártok vezetőit Paksra, hogy tájékoztassa őket a Duna vízszintjének duzzasztásához szükséges védelmi munkák folyamatairól, senki sem fogadta el a meghívását. A Fidesz kommunikációs igazgatója, Havasi Bertalan szombaton rövid közleményben reagált a miniszterelnökre. Azt írta, bebizonyosodott, hogy helyes döntés volt a távolmaradás Magyar Péter paksi „önfényező Facebook-bohóckodásától”. Az MTI-hez eljuttatott közlemény szerint az esemény a „miniszterelnök politikai őrjöngéséről szólt”, amit szánalmasnak nevezett. Toroczkai László, a Mi Hazánk elnöke az X-en reagált , ő azért nem vett részt a paksi körbejáráson, mert jelenleg a gyerekeivel nyaral. Toroczkai szerint Magyar Péter a tegnap este küldött levelében jelezte, hogy a meghívás kizárólag a parlamenti pártelnököknek szólt, így helyette Tóth Máté energiajogászt nem delegálhatja. Tóth egyébként Paksra utazott, de a helyszínre nem engedték be. „Ezzel világossá tette, hogy a pártelnökök meghívásával nem a szakmai javaslatok egyeztetése volt a célja, csak a hangulatkeltés. Így pedig akkor sem segítettünk volna Magyarországnak, ha minden pártelnök elmegy” – írta Toroczkai. A Mi Hazánk korábban Tóthot jelölte köztársasági elnöknek , aki a párt szerint független, ugyanakkor számos Fidesz-közeli helyen megfordult. Németh Szilárd és Dömötör Csaba mellett ő is fellelhető a Rezsivédelmi Digitális Polgári Kör alapítói között , illetve feltűnt a Megafonhoz tartozó Patrióta YouTube-csatornán is, ahol arról győzködte a nézőket, hogy a 2026. januárban tapasztalt hideg téli időjárás megkérdőjelezi a liberális újságírók és aktivisták által terjesztett „klímanarratívát”. A miniszterelnök a paksi tájékoztatóra meghívta Orbán Viktort, valamint a többi parlamenti párt vezetőjét is Paksra, hogy tájékoztassa őket „az évtizedek óta nem látott építkezés részleteiről, továbbá a korábbi évek mulasztásairól, amelyek szükségessé tették a beavatkozást”. Toroczkai László már tegnap jelezte, hogy nem utazik Paksra szabadsága miatt, Havasi Bertalan, a Fidesz kommunikációs igazgatója a Népszava kérdésére válaszolt a miniszterelnök meghívására, azt írta, „a pártelnökök nem Magyar Péter politikai biodíszletei”. https://www.thedailybeast.com/putin-and-.text: By Tom Latchem Published Oct 12, 2026 6:38AM EDT Vladimir Putinâs forces bombarded Ukrainian energy facilities within hours of Donald Trumpâs boast that he had secured a partial ceasefire. Trump, 80, announced Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to immediately stop attacking each otherâs energy infrastructure. While providing no details of the supposed breakthrough, he declared on Truth Social that the two countries had reached an agreement. âBoth parties have agreed. Do not break it!â the U.S. president wrote. ADVERTISEMENT Except nobody else seems to have got the memo. Donald Trump claims to have brokered a deal between Ukraine and Russia. Truth Social/Donald Trump Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Trumpâs announcement, which Moscow had not publicly confirmed, caught him by surprise. ADVERTISEMENT Zelensky, 48, said the purported agreement had been ânews to me,â while insisting Ukraine would halt strikes against Russian energy targets only if Moscow reciprocated. Get the Best of the Beast Sign Up for The Swamp Newsletter By clicking â SUBSCRIBE â you agree to our Terms of Use and Privacy Policy . By Monday, he was openly mocking Trumpâs demands. Zelensky told the Warsaw Security Forum that Putin, 74, apparently âdoes not read Truth Socialâ after Russian forces attacked a power station in Kharkiv almost immediately after Trumpâs declaration. Trump and Zelensky have a complicated history. The Washington Post/The Washington Post via Getty Im The attacks continued overnight, leaving Ukrainians without electricity and damaging infrastructure across several regions. In Izyum, northeastern Ukraine, residents were left without power after Russian strikes damaged the local electricity network, the BBC reported . Railway and electricity installations were also attacked in the western Zhytomyr region, where firefighters battled blazes from repeated Russian strikes, the outlet said. A rescuer takes shelter in an entrance of an apartment building amid the threat of another Russian drone strike. Sofiia Gatilova/REUTERS/Sofiia Gatilova In a separate attack on Sunday evening, a Russian drone strike killed three people and injured nine, including children, in the village of Pisochyn, according to the Associated Press . European leaders expressed doubts about Trumpâs announcement. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Monday that the bloc would welcome a ceasefire once Russia demonstrated it was observing one. FROM RUSSIA WITH LOVE Trump Cuts Desperate Deal With Putin to Save MAGA's Skin Sarah Ewall-Wice The apparent diplomatic failure came just days after Trump agreed to ease sanctions against Russia as part of a deal intended to release Russian diesel onto global markets, as he struggles with soaring fuel prices ahead of Novemberâs midterm elections. The president has blamed Ukrainian attacks against Russian refineries for worsening the global shortage, despite the damage to energy supplies caused by his own war with Iran. Play Video But the Kremlin reportedly offered no concessions toward ending its invasion during Trumpâs Friday phone conversation with Putin. Instead, the Russian leader maintained his demands while Trump publicly suggested Ukraine needed a new president. It was not the first time Trump had prematurely proclaimed progress. He announced a similar energy truce in September, but fighting continued. By Monday morning, there had been no reported public confirmation from Moscow that it had agreed to the latest ceasefire. https://www.dw.com/en/36-years-later-hun.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5P4iW Prefer DW on Google Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar made releasing the documents a campaign pledge Image: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP Advertisement On November 4, 1956, tens of thousands of Soviet soldiers and tanks swept into Hungary , brutally suppressing the country's anti-Communist uprising. Decades of dictatorship followed, relying on Hungary's brutal secret police to keep the system in place. Events on Nov. 4 this year represent something of a reckoning with this dark chapter of Hungarian history. Prime Minister Peter Magyar's government is ordering the full release of the country's secret police "agent files," which contain the names of Hungarian state security informants, some of whom cooperated out of their own volition even as others passed on information unwittingly. In 1956, Hungarians tried to stop Soviet tanks with cobble stone barricades Image: AP Photo/picture alliance Magyar and his Tisza party had previously promised to make the "agent files" public if elected. Their release is an historic event, as it comes after over three decades of heated debate over how to handle such sensitive files. The decision to publish is also sure to spark further debate on Communist-era guilt and responsibility. Release opposed for years Hungarians have been calling for the release of the files for years. After the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 and the end of Soviet rule, civil rights activists and smaller Hungarian political parties said the files should be released. Demands for their publication were expressed repeatedly over following decades. Yet Hungary's first post-Communist prime minister Jozsef Antall, a conservative, rejected the idea as did Viktor Orban 's long-ruling Fidesz party. The latter blocked efforts to open the files, voting more than 30 times against such plans since 2010, according to Hungarian news platform Telex. A partial release of state security files did occur in the 1990s, when the Hungarian parliament passed the so-called "agents law" in 1994. This required members of the government, members of parliament and certain public servants to undergo background checks to determine whether they had ever worked for the former state security services. From 1997, Hungarian citizens have been able to view their own files and in 2003, permissions were expanded. But they have never been able to find out the names of informants. The law relevant to the files contained provisions that were open to broad interpretation, which allowed government agencies such as the Ministry of Interior to prevent the transfer of files from the secret police to the Historical Archives of the Hungarian State Security, or ABTL, if they believed it would compromise national security. Such a selective release of files not only prevented Hungarian society from learning the truth about its state security service, it also made it possible for files to be exploited in political power struggles, for example, by leaking compromising information about politicians to the public. Viktor Orban's Fidesz party never supported making the 'agent files' public Image: Balint Szentgallay/NurPhoto/picture alliance One such case involved former Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Medgyessy, who was exposed by the Fidesz-affiliated daily Magyar Nemzet in 2002 for having worked as a Communist-era secret agent. Political fallout expected Magyar's government is putting an end to this. From Nov. 4, databases containing all the names of, and key information about, informants will be made available online. Additional databases will be released as well. They include one of the most extensive databases on individuals recruited to work for the Hungarian state security agency. Confidentiality provisions set out in the old "agent law" have also been scaled back, meaning significantly more files will likely be accessible in the future. The upcoming release of data on up to 60,000 out of an estimated 150,000 secret police informants could have major political consequences. Even so, ABTL director Bendeguz Gergo Cseh recently cautioned that, "you can't believe everything the state security agencies and their files claim." Many documents were incomplete and not fully reliable and many files had been destroyed, he said. Others are also skeptical about the release. Historian Janos M. Rainer, an expert on Hungary's dictatorship, told Telex that the publication would have made sense right after the fall of the regime. Releasing the files after all these years is more of a symbolic gesture, he argued. Meanwhile historian Krisztian Ungvary, who has researched the state security files extensively, welcomes the upcoming publication. It will allow historians to pursue new research and society to engage in fresh debates, Ungvary told DW. He believes Hungary will benefit from such reflection, as "societal lies inevitably lead to a strained relationship with politics and the price we paid for that was 16 years of Fidesz rule." Defendants are questioned by a judge in Budapest on March 9, 1957, during the first show trial held after the 1956 Hungarian uprising Image: MTI/picture alliance Political reckoning For Magyar, making this information public carries great significance. The idea of coming to terms with the past, especially the years of the Orban regime, is one of his favorite topics. When the Hungarian parliament amended the law about the files in mid-September, Magyar wrote on Facebook that, "after a 36-year delay, the Hungarian parliament today decided, at the initiative of Tisza, to make the 'agent files' public. Fidesz did not support the motion. I wonder why?" It was an allusion to the fact that many prominent figures in Fidesz' ranks and in Orban's inner circle were members of the Hungarian Communist party or secret police. The most well-known of the latter is likely Jozsef Horvath, a former full-time employee of the department of Hungarian state security that was responsible for suppressing the domestic opposition. Under Orban, Horvath worked as an intelligence officer and security advisor, and in 2024, he became the research director of Orban's Sovereignty Protection Office. This was an agency that exposed supposed enemies of the Orban regime, branding them " foreign agents ." This article was originally published in German. https://www.themoscowtimes.com/2026/10/2.text: Oct. 29, 2026 Construction on the Baltic Defense Line. RKIK / Hendrik Tali Estonia plans to construct 150 bunkers along its northeastern border with Russia’s Leningrad region as part of a broader Baltic defense initiative, the public broadcaster ERR reported Wednesday. “One hundred of them will be on state land, and around 50 on municipal or private land,” Estonian Defense Minister Martin Herem reportedly told lawmakers. Herem said the government is negotiating agreements with private landowners in the northeastern county of Ida-Viru, with options ranging from compensation to long-term leases and direct property buyouts. The installations will form the so-called Baltic Defense Line, an agreement that Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania announced in 2024 to build a series of bunkers along their borders with Russia and Belarus to defend against potential attacks. Earlier this month, the Financial Times reported that Estonia, a nation of 1.3 million people, had pivoted toward an “active defense” strategy after studying Russia’s military tactics in Ukraine. Under the updated doctrine, Estonia has been relocating primary combat units to towns along the border with the Leningrad region. In Narva, construction is underway for facilities that can house up to 1,000 soldiers during a crisis situation. Kremlin officials have downplayed the Estonian troop movements near the border while asserting that Russian intelligence maintains full surveillance over NATO deployments along the frontier.
